headline: Point Bass Have Gone to Bed With the Sun — Eels After Dark Are the Play
subhead: Daytime's quiet at the Lighthouse, but the night shift is loaded, and the albie clock is ticking toward the August 12 new moon.
body_markdown:
There's a rhythm to August out here that never changes, not in fifty years of watching this water. The Point goes to sleep in the daylight and wakes up hard after dark, and that's exactly what's happening right now. Montauk's holding at 69.1 degrees, which by East End standards is cool and clean for this time of year — but it's still enough to push that warm surface layer down over the reef, and the bass have responded the way they always do: they've gone deep, they've gone nocturnal, and if you're fishing the Lighthouse rip at high noon expecting daytime blitzes, you're going to go home disappointed.

I've been running the boulder field off the North Bar at first light and again at last light for two weeks now, and the pattern's holding. On the building tide — that two-hour window before and after the turn — the bass are stacking up tight to the rocks in 15 to 25 feet, and they want an eel. Not a swim shad, not a bucktail in daylight — a live eel, snelled on a 7/0 short-shank hook, drifted right along the boulder seams where the current breaks. We've had fish to 38 pounds off that stretch this week, mostly between 9 p.m. and 2 a.m., and every one of them came on the incoming when the rip was really running. During the day, if you want a shot, go subsurface with a bunker chunk on a fish-finder rig and fish it deep and slow off the Elbow — you'll pick at fish, but it's not the show it'll be after the sun drops.

Bluefish are the daylight consolation prize, and they're not shy about it. Shagwong Reef has been holding good numbers of choppers in the 8-to-12-pound class, working bait schools in 30 to 40 feet on the last of the outgoing. Umbrella rigs and diamond jigs both work, but if you want to have some fun with them, throw topwater poppers into the boils — they're feeding aggressively enough right now that you don't need finesse, you need presence. This is the tail end of that northern push everybody's been talking about all month, and it's still paying off out here even as it winds down elsewhere.

Fluke fishing has been the honest, dependable piece of the puzzle. It's not blitz-level — I want to be straight with you about that — but it's steady, and steady is a good word in August. We flagged this exact pattern last week: keepers mixed with shorts on the structure-oriented drifts, and that's precisely what Turtle Cove and the sandy stretches off the south side beaches have given up. Five-inch white Gulp Swimming Mullets on ¾-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom in 25 to 35 feet, have been the ticket, with a few nicer fish — four and five pounds — coming off the drop-offs adjacent to structure on the last two hours of the outgoing. If you're grinding for dinner fish, this is where I'd put my time during daylight hours while we wait on the bass to wake back up.

Offshore, the bottom fishing has been genuinely excellent — porgies thick on the structure in 50 to 60 feet with squid strips and clam, and sea bass mixed in on the same drops for anyone willing to run out past the Point and soak bait on the rockpiles. It's not glamorous, but it's meat in the cooler on days when the surf isn't cooperating, and right now it's about as sure a thing as this beat has to offer.

Now, the piece everybody's really asking about at the dock: albies and bonito. We called this one — said the building tide cycle off the July 29 full moon, stacked against the calendar, put us in a 10-to-14-day arrival window, and that window is very much open right now. I haven't had a confirmed albie in the boat yet, but the signs are lining up the way they always do right before Montauk lights the fuse — bait's getting nervous around the rips, there's bunched-up peanut bunker showing off the south side, and the water's holding that clean, cool edge that albies and bonito like to run right along. This place is usually first in the region to turn it on once the fish commit, and with the new moon building on August 12, I'd have my epoxy jigs and Deadly Dicks rigged and ready by this weekend, not next week.

Looking ahead, I don't expect a dramatic shift in the next 48 hours — the bass will keep doing their deep, nocturnal thing, the blues will keep working Shagwong on the outgoing, and fluke will keep paying steady dividends on the south side drifts. But by the 72-hour mark, as that new moon tide starts building real strength, I'd be watching the surface off the Point and North Bar closely for the first albie showings. If a front doesn't come through and mix things up, this is the window. My money's on the boulder field after dark for bass this week, and my eyes are on the horizon for the first fin cutting through bait on the surface — because when Montauk turns that corner, it doesn't ease into it. It happens fast, and you want to already be rigged when it does.
